text:
Help me write a case for my promotion. I'm the assistant front office manager at a 180-room hotel, and the front office manager job is open. I'm applying, and my general manager wants it in writing by Friday.

Facts:
- I've worked here 6 years, the last 2 as assistant manager.
- Our guest score for check-in on the main review site went from 7.9 to 8.6 over the last 18 months. The lobby and all the rooms were renovated during the same time.
- I rewrote the front desk training. New hires now work the desk alone after 5 shifts instead of 9.
- Front desk turnover was 9 of 14 people in the year before I became assistant manager, and 5 of 14 last year.
- I've covered the front office manager's job alone for the 7 weeks since she left.
- I have never managed a budget. The front office manager owns a $1.1 million payroll budget.

I want it to say I'm the main reason our guest scores went up. One page.

Before I draft this, there's one problem with the main claim, and I have some questions that would make the case stronger.

## The scores claim

**What you want to say:** you're the main reason the check-in score went from 7.9 to 8.6.

**What your facts support:** the score went up while you were running a better-trained and more stable desk team. But the lobby and every room were renovated in the same 18 months, and your GM approved that renovation. The first thing they'll think when they read "main reason" is "what about the renovation?" Your facts can't answer that yet. If the claim looks overstated, the GM may start doubting the rest of the page too.

**A version your facts do support:** "Over the same 18 months that check-in scores rose from 7.9 to 8.6, I rebuilt the team that does the checking in. New hires now work the desk alone after 5 shifts instead of 9, and turnover fell from 9 of 14 to 5 of 14." That ties the score to your work without saying you caused all of it. It leaves the GM to make the connection, and they're more likely to believe a conclusion they reach themselves.

You may have facts that would let you go further (see question 1). You decide which version to use.

## How I'd build the case

- **Claim:** you should be the next front office manager.
- **Grounds:**
  - You've done the job alone for 7 weeks.
  - Front desk turnover fell from 64% to 36%.
  - Training time is down 44%.
  - Check-in scores rose.
  - You have 6 years at this hotel.
- **What connects the facts to the claim:** the best evidence that someone can run the department is that they already are, and that the team got better under them.
- **The GM's main objection:** the $1.1M payroll budget, which you've never managed. The page has to say this openly and answer it. If it doesn't, the GM will raise it for you.

## Questions

1. **Did check-in improve more than the categories the renovation affected?** Compare check-in with rooms, cleanliness or comfort. If check-in rose more, or rose after your new training started, that's real evidence for a stronger claim. When did the new training start?
2. **What have you done that touches payroll?** That could be scheduling, approving overtime, or watching labor hours, especially in the last 7 weeks. And what can you commit to on learning the budget? For example, a course, or regular reviews with the GM or the finance person. It has to be something you'll actually do. I won't make one up.
3. **What happened during the 7 weeks you've been covering?** Anything you can count helps: scores held or rising, no gaps in the schedule, problems you settled, tasks you took on.
4. **What does your GM already think of you?** Have they raised any concerns, and are they also looking at outside candidates?
5. **Names and date:** the GM's name, the name you'll sign with, and the date you'll hand it in.
6. **Is there anything the GM knows, or will find out, that you haven't mentioned?** For example, a weak number, a complaint, or something that slipped. It's better to deal with it on the page than have it come up afterwards.

You can answer whichever of these you know. I'll write the one-page case from your answers without guessing at the ones you skip.

1. I don't have the comparison with the other categories. I do know the renovation started 5 months into the 18 months, and check-in had already gone from 7.9 to 8.2 before it started. I don't remember exactly when the new training started. And I'm fine with the version that says what I did instead of "main reason."

2. In the 7 weeks I've been covering, overtime came in under the monthly plan. I can commit to finishing the company's finance course in my first 3 months (the company pays for it). I can also commit to weekly sessions on the payroll budget with our controller, Ben Oduya. He's already offered.

3. No front desk shift went uncovered in the 7 weeks.

4. I don't know if he has concerns. There is an outside candidate, and I can't match their experience at a larger hotel.

5. GM is Mark Ellison. I'll sign as Daniela Ruiz. Handing it in Friday.

6. Check-in waits on Friday evenings are still the most common complaint at the desk.

I've written the version you chose. It says what you did and doesn't say you caused the whole rise in the score. Your answer to question 1 helped a lot: check-in had already reached 8.2 before the renovation started, so the renovation can't explain all of the gain. That number goes right next to the score.

<final_document>
**To:** Mark Ellison, General Manager
**From:** Daniela Ruiz, Assistant Front Office Manager
**Date:** Friday, November 20, 2026
**Re:** Application for Front Office Manager

Mark,

I'm applying for the front office manager position. I've been doing the job alone for the last seven weeks, so you've already seen how the department runs with me in charge. This is my case.

**I've been doing the job for seven weeks.** Since the position opened, I've run the front office on my own. No front desk shift has gone uncovered, and overtime has come in under the monthly plan.

**The desk is stronger than it was two years ago.**

- **Turnover:** In the year before I became assistant manager, 9 of our 14 front desk staff left. Last year, 5 of 14 left.
- **Training:** I rewrote our front desk training. New hires now work the desk alone after 5 shifts instead of 9.
- **Guest scores:** Our check-in score on the main review site rose from 7.9 to 8.6 over the last 18 months. The renovation helped, but it doesn't explain the whole rise. Check-in had already reached 8.2 before work started, five months into that period. I'm not claiming the whole increase, but the team checking guests in is the team I trained and kept.

**The budget is the part I haven't done yet.** The front office manager owns a $1.1 million payroll budget, and I have never managed one. Keeping overtime under plan for seven weeks is the closest I've come, and I know that isn't the same thing. If I get the role, I commit to:

- completing the company's finance course within my first three months, and
- meeting weekly with Ben Oduya on the payroll budget. He has already offered to do this.

**On experience.** You may be considering candidates who have worked at larger hotels, and I can't match that. What I bring is six years at this hotel, a front desk team I trained, and seven weeks of results in this exact role. You wouldn't have to wait for me to learn the property, the staff or our guests.

**What I'd work on first.** Friday evening check-in waits are still the most common complaint at our desk. It's the first problem I'd take on as front office manager.

I'd welcome the chance to talk through any of this before you decide.

Thank you,

Daniela Ruiz
</final_document>

A few things to check before Friday:

- **Friday evening waits:** I said this is the first problem you'd take on, but I left out how, because you didn't give me a plan. If you have one, add a sentence. Something like "add a second agent from 5 to 8 p.m." is the kind of detail that would help. If "the first problem I'd take on" goes further than you want to commit, change it.
- **The 7.9 to 8.2 rise:** You don't remember when the new training started, so the memo doesn't say the training caused that early rise. It only puts the number next to your work.
- **Review site:** I wrote "the main review site." If Mark would expect its name, add it.
- **Date:** I took "Friday" to mean November 20.

I left out your training numbers worked out as percentages (turnover went from 64% to 36%, and training time fell by 44%). The plain counts are easier to check, and Mark can do the math.
